questions.solution:
• Motion refers to the change in the position of an object with respect to its surroundings over a period of time.

Further Insight:

• Motion refers to the change in position of an object with respect to its surroundings over a period of time.

• The motion of an object with mass can be described using key parameters like distance, displacement, speed, velocity, time, and acceleration.

• A pendulum exhibits oscillatory motion as it swings back and forth around its central position, repeating this motion at regular intervals.

Further Insight:

• The type of motion depends on the forces acting on the object. The primary types are:

• Translational Motion: Movement of an object along a path in any of the three dimensions.

• Rotational Motion: Circular motion around a fixed axis.

• Linear Motion: A form of translational motion where the object moves in a straight line.

• Periodic Motion: Motion that repeats itself at regular intervals (e.g., the motion of a pendulum).

• Simple Harmonic Motion: A type of periodic motion where a restoring force, proportional to displacement, acts in the opposite direction (e.g., pendulum).

• Projectile Motion: Motion with both horizontal and vertical displacement.

• Oscillatory Motion: Repetitive motion around a central point, often mechanical, referred to as vibration.

• Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of the car, which, in this case, is zero.

○ The car ends up at the same position it started from, so displacement is zero, though the distance traveled is 200 meters

Further Insight:

• Distance and Displacement

• Distance:

○ Total path length covered by an object.

○ it is a scalar quantity (only magnitude).

• Displacement:

○ Shortest path between two points (starting and final position) with both magnitude and direction.

○ Displacement can be zero, but distance cannot.

questions.solution:
• Velocity is a vector quantity because it has both magnitude and direction.

• Speed is a scalar quantity as it lacks direction.

• Mass is a scalar and has no direction.

• Time is always a scalar, measured in units like seconds.

Further Insight:

• Newton's Three Laws of Motion

○ Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia):

■ This law states that an object will continue in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force.

■ This law defines the concept of inertia, which is the tendency of objects to resist changes in their state of motion.

■ Example: A book lying on a table will remain there until someone applies a force to move it.

○ Newton's Second Law (Law of Acceleration):

■ According to this law, the rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied external force, and this change occurs in the direction of the force.

■ Mathematically, it is expressed as: F=ma, Where F is the force, m is the mass, and a is the acceleration.

■ This law explains how the force applied to an object determines its acceleration.

■ Example: A heavier object requires more force to accelerate at the same rate as a lighter object.

○ Newton's Third Law (Action and Reaction):

■ Newton's Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

• This means that if an object exerts a force on another object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first object.

■ Example: walking on earth

• Acceleration is a vector quantity.

• Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes over time.

• Negative acceleration is often called deceleration.

Further Insight:

• Acceleration

○ Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity of an object with respect to time.

○ It is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction.

○ If the velocity of an object changes, either in magnitude (speed) or direction, the object is said to be accelerating.

• Formula:

Where:

○ a = acceleration

○ v = final velocity

○ u = initial velocity

○ t = time taken for the change

• Unit: The SI unit of acceleration is m/s².

• Types of Acceleration:

○ Positive Acceleration: When an object speeds up.

○ Negative Acceleration (Deceleration): When an object slows down.

○ Uniform Acceleration: When velocity changes at a constant rate.

○ Non-uniform Acceleration: When velocity changes at varying rates.

• Distance, being the total path length, can never be zero.

• Displacement is the shortest path and can be less than or equal to the distance but not always equal.

• Displacement is a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction.

Further Insight:

Displacement

CriteriaDistanceDisplacement
DefinitionThe total length of the path traveled by an object, irrespective of direction.The shortest straight line between the initial and final positions of an object.
Type of QuantityScalar (only magnitude)Vector (magnitude and direction)
MagnitudeAlways positive, non-zeroCan be positive, negative, or zero
PathDepends on the actual path takenDepends only on the initial and final positions
FormulaSum of all paths traveledDisplacement=Final Position - Initial position
UnitMeters (m)Meters (m)
ValueAlways equal to or greater than displacementAlways equal to or less than distance

Type of GraphAxes (Y vs X)Slope RepresentsExplanation
Distance-Time GraphDistance (Y) vs Time (X)SpeedThe slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed of an object. A steeper slope indicates higher speed.
